# In Praise of Getting Lost

Some of the best parts of my life have begun with a turn taken for no good reason. Not with a grand decision, not with a well-planned journey, but with a street closed, a missed turning, or the simple impulse to see what lay beyond a familiar row of buildings. I once got off a bus two stops early because the afternoon was too beautiful to spend indoors. The neighborhood was unfamiliar, the shops were shabby, and I had no idea where I was going. By dusk, I had found a tiny cinema, eaten dumplings from a place with no English sign, and watched the streetlights flicker on above a courtyard where someone was practicing the trumpet badly and happily. It was, in every practical sense, a mistake. It remains one of my favorite memories.

We are taught to regard getting lost as a failure of navigation. Maps, GPS coordinates, and turn-by-turn instructions have made wandering nearly frictionless, and we have responded by eliminating almost every opportunity to wander. We know which lane to take before leaving home. We know where to park before setting out. We know, often, how long the journey will take, how much fuel it will consume, and whether there will be traffic. Convenience is wonderful, and I do not want to return to a world in which every trip requires a paper map unfolded and refolded in the rain. Still, efficiency has a hidden cost. When we know exactly where we are going, we may arrive everywhere without having visited any of it.

Being lost and being directionless are not the same thing. The person who is lost once had a destination, or at least expected to have one. The directionless person has temporarily released the need to arrive. One is a small failure of certainty; the other can be a deliberate form of freedom. We rarely grant ourselves permission to be without an objective. We schedule our days around errands, our conversations around points, and our conversations around the possibility of future productivity. Even our rest is optimized: ten minutes of meditation, thirty minutes of walking, perhaps a carefully curated playlist intended to improve our focus. We have become skilled at going places without being there.

This is why childhood is full of getting lost. Children disappear into neighborhoods with the confidence of explorers because nobody has yet taught them to calculate the cost of a wrong turn. A backyard becomes a continent. A drainpipe is a mountain. The space behind a hedge may contain pirates, dinosaurs, a buried treasure, or a secret entrance to another world. Children do not need to make every moment meaningful. They simply encounter it, and their attention is intense enough to turn an ordinary patch of ground into a place of mystery. Somewhere along the way, adults begin correcting this. “Stay where I can see you.” “Don’t wander off.” “How did you get lost?” These phrases are usually sensible, but they gradually replace curiosity with caution.

Modern navigation makes sense of this transformation. A phone can tell us to turn left in five hundred feet, then right after passing a gas station. It can reassure us that we are still on the right path, even when the scenery is strange. At first, this feels like liberation. But a route is not the same as an experience. The map tells us the name of a street while missing the smell of bread from its basement window, the uneven rhythm of its pavement, the old woman sitting on a stoop, and the cat watching us from a wall. It tells us where to go while overlooking why we might want to go there at all. We arrive efficiently and discover that we have skipped the journey.

Perhaps this is why travel can be more memorable when something goes wrong. The planned day is pleasant, but the day the train stops, the flight is canceled, or the address cannot be found acquires a strange intensity. We notice the waiting room. We study the other passengers. We learn the particular boredom of an afternoon with nowhere to be. We notice the station café because we had never thought to enter it. Misfortunes interrupt our habit of taking the world for granted. Even inconvenience becomes a kind of tour guide, pointing out details that efficiency had made invisible.

There is a practical wisdom in the old stories about travelers who are advised to follow the path. The instruction is always the same: do not stray from the road, do not trust the shortcuts, do not be tempted by the beautiful view. The implication is that the world beyond the path is dangerous, or at least unproductive. This is useful advice when a storm is approaching or a region is unsafe. It is less useful as a philosophy of life. We may need clear paths sometimes, but the world is larger than the routes we have drawn across it. A life spent only moving from obligation to obligation can become a life spent not living at all.

To be lost is also to experience a kind of humility. We are not as in control as our plans suggest. The bus will not always arrive. The remembered shortcut may have disappeared. The person we asked for directions may not know either. In such moments, the usual hierarchy between the person who knows and the person who does not becomes briefly comic. We all become beginners again. We look up at unfamiliar signs, try to read the landscape, and ask other people what they think. Humility is often described as a spiritual virtue, but it can arrive through something as ordinary as missing a stop.

Asking for directions is one of the simplest acts of vulnerability. We must admit that we are in a place we do not understand. We must accept help from a stranger, and we must temporarily place our sense of self in someone else’s hands. The conversation is usually brief. “Excuse me, is this the road to the river?” “Keep going, then turn at the church.” The words are simple, but they create a small bridge between lives. The stranger has been here before. We have not. Their memory becomes our route, and our arrival will include them even though we may never learn their name.

There is something unexpectedly intimate about being lost in a city. The city that seemed anonymous becomes specific. We notice where people buy their lunch, which streets have trees, where the footsteps become loud, where the light from a window falls across the pavement. The city stops being a backdrop and becomes a collection of human arrangements. Every block appears to have been made by someone who wanted to solve a problem: shelter, transport, commerce, beauty, privacy, conversation. Even the neglected corners reveal intentions. The empty lot may once have been a garden. The concrete bridge may have replaced a stream. A path through a fence may have been an informal agreement between neighbors.

This is one of the great pleasures of walking without a route. A destination gives us permission to ignore everything between the beginning and the end. A journey gives us other reasons to look. We can stop at a bakery because the door is open. We can take a street because a painted door is bright red. We can sit on a bench and watch pigeons fight over a crust. These choices do not lead to productivity, but they restore attention. The world becomes less like a problem to be solved and more like a relationship to be developed. Attention, in this sense, is not a spotlight we point at things. It is a form of affection.

I have come to think that many of our deepest attachments begin as acts of attention. We love particular people not because they possess every quality, but because we have noticed how they take a cup of tea, how they become quiet when embarrassed, how they laugh before they understand the joke. We love particular landscapes because we have watched them change across years. We love songs because we have carried them through repeated circumstances until the lyrics have become part of our biography. To pay attention is to allow something to matter more than it strictly needs to. Getting lost is simply one way of making that possible.

The world is full of systems designed to prevent this kind of attention. Search engines can tell us the answer before we have formed a question. Recommendation systems can tell us what we might like before we have experienced anything new. The feed presents an endless procession of things chosen by somebody else’s model of desire. We mistake movement for discovery, and variety for curiosity. A day can contain hundreds of images without giving us one memory. We may be exposed to everything while experiencing nothing in particular. The solution is not necessarily to abandon these tools, but to remember that tools can organize our attention without supplying it.

To wander is to make a modest resistance to this condition. Not a dramatic resistance, not a withdrawal from the world, but a willingness to be unguided for an afternoon. Take the long street. Walk without counting the minutes. Choose the market instead of the station. Sit somewhere you have never sat. Let the route depend on weather, conversation, or a change of mind. There is no need to turn wandering into a spiritual practice or a personality trait. Its value may be simpler: it reminds us that time can be spent without being spent on something else.

The best walks are often the ones that achieve nothing. We return home with no souvenir, no photograph, and no particularly useful story. Yet something has shifted. A street we had ignored has become a place we know. A mistake has revealed a preference. A period of uncertainty has allowed an idea to surface that would otherwise have remained buried. Sometimes we need to stop answering the question “How do I get there?” in order to ask the more interesting question, “What becomes possible when I am not on my way?”

This does not mean that uncertainty is always beneficial. A person lost in a dangerous place may need help, and a person who is driving through a snowstorm should not treat navigation as an experiment. The celebration of wandering becomes irresponsible if it ignores real differences in safety and privilege. Not everyone can afford to miss a train, wander away from a support system, or follow an unexplained path. To speak freely about getting lost is also to recognize that most of us are surrounded by maps, resources, and directions that others may not have.

Even within those limits, however, we can practice small uncertainties. Read a book without rushing toward its conclusion. Walk through a familiar park by a route you have never chosen. Allow a conversation to continue without steering it toward an objective. Learn the name of a street merely because you have crossed it many times without knowing what it was called. These acts are tiny, almost invisible. They are not escapes from responsibility. They are ways of remembering that a life is not solely a sequence of completed objectives.

There is also a form of getting lost that has nothing to do with geography. We can lose ourselves in a book, a piece of music, a conversation, or an idea. The world may continue outside, but for a while we do not notice it. The hours pass. The body remains seated, while the mind travels elsewhere. This kind of disappearance is one of the reasons stories matter. Fiction gives us permission to inhabit lives that are not ours, to cross borders without passports, to experience losses and victories that belong to other people. A good novel does not confuse us about reality. It enlarges reality by showing us how many other ways of seeing it might exist.

Children often seem naturally capable of this kind of imaginative travel. They do not require a plot to explain why they are spending time with a cardboard box. The box can be a boat, a house, a hospital, or a machine for traveling to the moon. Their boredom is not empty. It is the space in which invention begins. It may look like nothing from the outside: a child sitting alone, moving a small object across the floor. Inside, the room has become a theater. We should be careful not to romanticize childhood or hold adults to impossible standards, but we can remember that boredom is not always a problem requiring immediate correction.

We often rush to fill every pause because silence makes us uncomfortable. We reach for our phones before the elevator arrives. We turn on the radio in the car even when we do not need company. We seek constant stimulation as though stillness were a warning. Yet the mind, given a little room, may produce its own material. It may remember a forgotten conversation, notice a pattern in ordinary events, or construct a plan for something we had believed impossible. The empty moment is not necessarily unproductive. It may be where the next thought enters.

A garden offers a useful example. If we plant seeds and then check them every minute, we may disturb the process. We can water them, protect them, and make sure they receive light, but we must also wait. The waiting is part of the relationship. We cannot force a flower to bloom by staring at its stem. In the same way, certain parts of our inner lives develop at their own pace. We may not know what we are becoming until the conditions are right. Aimlessness, properly understood, is not the same as giving up. It is allowing growth to exceed the timetable we imagined for it.

The phrase “lost in translation” suggests another kind of dislocation. We may lose a word, a joke, an emotion, or a piece of our own history. Language fails us. The sentence we had carefully prepared comes out differently in another language. The explanation we expected to clarify a misunderstanding instead makes it worse. We lose the path back to what we meant. Yet the awkwardness can be productive. When words stop working perfectly, we begin to notice tone, gesture, context, and silence. Translation becomes an act of interpretation rather than substitution. We discover that meaning is not a package that can be carried unchanged from one person to another.

A similar thing happens in music when a melody is separated from its lyrics. We know a tune that once carried one meaning, and now it belongs to a different room, a different year, a different person. The song is still recognizable, but the feeling has changed. Memory is not an archive. It is an ongoing arrangement. We may lose the original context, but we do not lose the experience of having known it. Sometimes the meaning that remains is stranger and more valuable than the meaning we first assigned.

To be lost is therefore to encounter the limits of certainty. We are always interpreting the world, and every interpretation may be partial. The route we have drawn is one route among many. The story we tell about our lives is one story among several. The person we believe ourselves to be may change when circumstances force us to choose a different street. This can be unsettling, but it can also be liberating. We are not obligated to remain faithful to every earlier version of ourselves.

One of the great reliefs of wandering is that it does not demand a performance. There is no need to look impressive, knowledgeable, or efficient. We may walk slowly. We may ask a child to point out the way. We may admit that we have no idea what happens at the end of the road. When we are not trying to impress anyone, our relation to the place becomes more honest. We can be interested without pretending to understand. We can be delighted by something without immediately knowing whether it is useful. Wonder is a form of knowledge, though not the kind that can be entered into a spreadsheet.

Many people describe travel as a way of finding themselves. Sometimes that is true, but I prefer to think of it as a way of finding out how many selves are possible. A person may be confident in one environment and hesitant in another. One city may bring out our sociability; another may bring out our patience. A solitary week may reveal a capacity for solitude we did not know we possessed. A crowded journey may teach us that companionship can exist without constant conversation. We do not discover a fixed essence. We discover that we can change shape without losing continuity.

I have met people whose stories begin with an accidental detour. They took a wrong train and found the town where they later studied art. They missed the last bus and met the friend who changed their career. They wandered into a lecture instead of a lecture and discovered a subject they now love. These stories can sound like fate in retrospect, but at the time they probably felt like inconvenience. The lesson is not that every mistake is a blessing. It is that a mistake does not have to be wasted.

Perhaps this is why the best stories rarely begin with perfect preparation. They begin with a disruption: a letter arrives unexpectedly, a stranger overhears something, a storm prevents a departure. The disruption makes room for a different future. If everything goes according to plan, the future may simply repeat the present. A little confusion gives the world an opening. It creates a space in which something unforeseen can enter. The person who never gets lost may never feel this opening, but neither may the person who uses getting lost as a way of avoiding responsibility. The gift lies not in confusion itself, but in what we do with it.

Our maps are useful for certain journeys, and our plans are useful for certain days. But we should not confuse them with the territory of a life. A map can show the river, but it cannot feel the water. It can show the mountain, but it cannot describe the relief of reaching the summit or the disappointment of arriving at the wrong one. The plan can provide structure, but it cannot tell us what the weather will do to our expectations. There must be room for the uncharted, even if the uncharted is only a few unfamiliar streets.

This is why I distrust the fantasy of a life fully known in advance. Such a fantasy sounds like freedom from uncertainty, but it is really freedom from surprise. It removes the possibility of being pleasantly interrupted. It makes every choice predictable and every day an extension of the day before. A little uncertainty is what keeps the future open. It keeps the world from becoming a closed system of obligations we have already agreed to perform. The detour is not always a deviation from the path. Sometimes it is the path itself.

In the evening, when I return from a walk without having intended to return, I often feel that I have crossed a border. Familiar streets have become briefly unfamiliar. I notice the moon between two buildings, the shape of a shadow, the sound of a bicycle chain. For a moment, the world seems to have rearranged itself while I was absent. Nothing has actually changed, except the arrangement of my attention. The walk has made the ordinary strange again.

I do not mean that ordinary life should be permanently strange. We need houses, schedules, meals, and people who can find us when we are needed. We need enough certainty to keep promises and enough structure to accomplish difficult things. But a life needs a little uncertainty to remain alive to possibility. Otherwise we may be so busy preserving our plans that we fail to notice the life happening around us.

When I put my phone away and walk without a destination, the effect is modest. I do not become wiser. I do not achieve enlightenment. I may still be hungry, late, or wearing the wrong shoes. But I return with a more vivid sense of the place. The world has been there all along, waiting to be noticed. Its details have not been waiting for me specifically, exactly. Yet attention makes them available. To pay attention is to discover that reality has been generously furnished for a great many people, and that we have only begun to look.

There is a particular freedom in not knowing which turn comes next. It releases us from the expectation that every choice must lead somewhere important. We can take the long way simply because it is long. We can sit beside a fountain without calculating how many minutes remain before we must leave. We can look at a blank wall and allow it to be blank. In a culture organized around acceleration, this freedom may seem almost subversive. It asks nothing of us except that we stop treating every moment as an opportunity to advance.

Over time, these small departures accumulate. They become a private geography, a map made not of destinations but of experiences. The street where someone gave us directions. The bench where we watched a summer storm. The bakery where the baker remembered our order. The path we found by accident and have returned to ever since. This map is invisible to anyone else, and that is part of its value. It records a relationship between a person and a place, not simply a sequence of coordinates.

The final pleasure of getting lost is that the return can feel like an arrival. We come back to familiar rooms, but they are not exactly as we left them. We have changed by a fraction. The world has changed by a fraction. Even if the street is still there and the bus still passes at the same time, the person crossing the threshold has been somewhere else. A walk without a destination may therefore return us to the destination differently. We are not lost forever. We are only reminded that being found is not the same as being finished.

In the end, I hope we can keep a little room in our lives for the wrong turn, the unasked street, the afternoon without an objective. Not as a form of carelessness, but as a form of openness. Not because the world needs us to be lost, but because we need the world to remain larger than our plan for it. A map is a useful companion. It can help us find our way and teach us where we are. But occasionally we should put it away, look up, and allow the unknown to become—not a threat, not a test, but an invitation.

We do not discover a fixed essence. We discover that we can change shape without losing continuity.

I have met people whose stories begin with an accidental detour. They took a wrong train and found the town where they later studied art. They missed the last bus and met the friend who changed their career. They wandered into a lecture instead of a lecture and discovered a subject they now love. These stories can sound like fate in retrospect, but at the time they probably felt like inconvenience. The lesson is not that every mistake is a blessing. It is that a mistake does not have to be wasted.

Perhaps this is why the best stories rarely begin with perfect preparation. They begin with a disruption: a letter arrives unexpectedly, a stranger overhears something, a storm prevents a departure. The disruption makes room for a different future. If everything goes according to plan, the future may simply repeat the present. A little confusion gives the world an opening. It creates a space in which something unforeseen can enter. The person who never gets lost may never feel this opening, but neither may the person who uses getting lost as a way of avoiding responsibility. The gift lies not in confusion itself, but in what we do with it.

Our maps are useful for certain journeys, and our plans are useful for certain days. But we should not confuse them with the territory of a life. A map can show the river, but it cannot feel the water. It can show the mountain, but it cannot describe the relief of reaching the summit or the disappointment of arriving at the wrong one. The plan can provide structure, but it cannot tell us what the weather will do to our expectations. There must be room for the uncharted, even if the uncharted is only a few unfamiliar streets.

This is why I distrust the fantasy of a life fully known in advance. Such a fantasy sounds like freedom from uncertainty, but it is really freedom from surprise. It removes the possibility of being pleasantly interrupted. It makes every choice predictable and every day an extension of the day before. A little uncertainty is what keeps the future open. It keeps the world from becoming a closed system of obligations we have already agreed to perform. The detour is not always a deviation from the path. Sometimes it is the path itself.

In the evening, when I return from a walk without having intended to return, I often feel that I have crossed a border. Familiar streets have become briefly unfamiliar. I notice the moon between two buildings, the shape of a shadow, the sound of a bicycle chain. For a moment, the world seems to have rearranged itself while I was absent. Nothing has actually changed, except the arrangement of my attention. The walk has made the ordinary strange again.

I do not mean that ordinary life should be permanently strange. We need houses, schedules, meals, and people who can find us when we are needed. We need enough certainty to keep promises and enough structure to accomplish difficult things. But a life needs a little uncertainty to remain alive to possibility. Otherwise we may be so busy preserving our plans that we fail to notice the life happening around us.

When I put my phone away and walk without a destination, the effect is modest. I do not become wiser. I do not achieve enlightenment. I may still be hungry, late, or wearing the wrong shoes. But I return with a more vivid sense of the place. The world has been there all along, waiting to be noticed. Its details have not been waiting for me specifically, exactly. Yet attention makes them available. To pay attention is to discover that reality has been generously furnished for a great many people, and that we have only begun to look.

There is a particular freedom in not knowing which turn comes next. It releases us from the expectation that every choice must lead somewhere important. We can take the long way simply because it is long. We can sit beside a fountain without calculating how many minutes remain before we must leave. We can look at a blank wall and allow it to be blank. In a culture organized around acceleration, this freedom may seem almost subversive. It asks nothing of us except that we stop treating every moment as an opportunity to advance.

Over time, these small departures accumulate. They become a private geography, a map made not of destinations but of experiences. The street where someone gave us directions. The bench where we watched a summer storm. The bakery where the baker remembered our order. The path we found by accident and have returned to ever since. This map is invisible to anyone else, and that is part of its value. It records a relationship between a person and a place, not simply a sequence of coordinates.

The final pleasure of getting lost is that the return can feel like an arrival. We come back to familiar rooms, but they are not exactly as we left them. We have changed by a fraction. The world has changed by a fraction. Even if the street is still there and the bus still passes at the same time, the person crossing the threshold has been somewhere else. A walk without a destination may therefore return us to the destination differently. We are not lost forever. We are only reminded that being found is not the same as being finished.

In the end, I hope we can keep a little room in our lives for the wrong turn, the unasked street, the afternoon without an objective. Not as a form of carelessness, but as a form of openness. Not because the world needs us to be lost, but because we need the world to remain larger than our plan for it. A map is a useful companion. It can help us find our way and teach us where we are. But occasionally we should put it away, look up, and allow the unknown to become—not a threat, not a test, but an invitation.
